newsitem.title: UK: Dlr stumbles in Europe, PPI quiets rate hike talk.
newsitem.headline: Dlr stumbles in Europe, PPI quiets rate hike talk.

text.p: The dollar dipped back below 1.70 marks in late Europe, shedding the bulk of its session gains after a shock drop in U.S. producer prices cast a damper on speculation of near-term Federal Reserve tightening.
Dollar/mark had spent most of the day on a firmer footing above 1.70, buoyed by comments suggesting the Bundesbank was happy with current levels.

Indications from German coalition sources of a hefty 1997 tax shortfall buoyed dollar/mark, but the 0.6 percent fall in U.S. April PPI -- the biggest drop since August 1993 -- deflated it as market rate rise speculation receded.
The market had been braced for unchanged overall PPI, while core prices confounded expectations of a 0.1 percent increase with a 0.1 percent fall.

"Most people seem to be of the view that the FOMC is too close to call. The producer prices will have encouraged a few more to believe there will be no Fed rate hike," said Adrian Owens, international economist at Julius Baer Investments.
The policy-making Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) next meets to decide rate policy on May 20.
The dollar was quoted at 1.7000/10 marks at 1544 GMT, off a 1.7085 high but up from late Tuesday's European level of 1.6964.

Bundesbank council member Ernst Welteke said earlier today that "it seems that a dollar rate at around 1.70 marks conforms with the real data". His colleague Klaus-Dieter Kuehbacher said later he believed current dollar/mark relations were good.
Dollar/yen slipped with dollar/mark in late Europe to trade at 118.26/36 at 1607 GMT versus Tuesday's close of 118.65/75. Dealers said intervention fears were keeping a cap around 120.

Cross moves, especially in mark/yen, cast their shadow on the dollar again, traders noted. Mark/yen hit an almost one-year low of 69.45 intraday and stood at 69.64/67 in late trade versus 69.97/00 around the same time yesterday.
"The mark/yen rate really is the 'big sell' when you compare relative policy trends in Europe and Japan," said Michael Burke, economist at Citibank in London.
Fear of higher Japanese rates -- together with a raft of yen-positive comments from Japanese officials -- last week helped trigger dollar/yen's biggest one-week fall since 1989.
Economic difficulties in Germany, however, mean there is little chance seen of rate tightening there.
"With the problems the Germans have got -- unemployment, strikes -- who'd want to buy marks?" said Peter Wood, forex trader at Bank of Boston here.
German economic woes were pointed up by government coalition sources, who told Reuters 1997 tax revenues would be nearly 20 billion marks less than forecast -- opening a huge budget hole.

Though that news cast doubt on Germany's chances of qualifying for European monetary union, Finance minister Theo Waigel said it would still make the grade. The government might, however, have to increase new borrowing for 1997 because of persistently high unemployment, Waigel said.
After today's PPI shock, the market is now awaiting U.S. April CPI tomorrow. U.S. industrial production, capacity utilization and real earnings are also due on Thursday.
The Philadelphia Fed survey for May and weekly jobless claims are due out, too. Friday sees the release of U.S. April housing starts and the May Michigan sentiment survey.
Elsewhere, sterling got a lift from robust UK unemployment figures for April, which showed the labour market tightening further but wage and earnings pressures easing.

UK jobless fell 59,400 for a rate of 5.9 percent against March's 6.1, while average earnings grew by 4.5 percent in the year to March. Sterling ended at 2.7885/00 marks and $1.6430/35 versus late Tuesday's 2.7685/00 and $1.6320/30.
-- Abigail Levene, London Newsroom +44-171-542-8968
